reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Presents as a groin swelling that appears or enlarges on standing, coughing, or straining and often reduces on lying flat

Indirect hernias travel down the inguinal canal along the spermatic cord and lie lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, while direct hernias push forward through a weakness in the posterior canal wall medial to those vessels
A hernia arising below and lateral to the pubic tubercle suggests a femoral hernia, whereas one above and medial to it suggests an inguinal hernia; this landmark helps distinguish the two
Reducibility, cough impulse, and whether the swelling can be controlled at the deep ring are key clinical assessments
Loss of cough impulse with a tense, tender, irreducible lump raises concern for obstruction or strangulation
Indirect hernias are the commonest groin hernia in both sexes and across all ages, reflecting a persistent processus vaginalis

Elective repair, most commonly tension-free mesh repair (open Lichtenstein or laparoscopic), is the definitive treatment; watchful waiting may be reasonable for small, minimally symptomatic hernias in selected patients
Chronic cough, constipation, bladder outflow obstruction, and heavy lifting raise intra-abdominal pressure and should be sought as contributing factors
reference.pathophysiology: An inguinal hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal. Indirect hernias pass through the deep (internal) inguinal ring into the canal, often through a patent processus vaginalis, and may descend into the scrotum. Direct hernias bulge forward through an attenuated posterior wall of the canal (Hesselbach's triangle) as a result of acquired weakness of the transversalis fascia. Raised intra-abdominal pressure and weakened abdominal wall connective tissue promote herniation. As a hernia enlarges the neck may narrow relative to the sac, predisposing to incarceration (irreducibility) and strangulation, in which the blood supply to trapped bowel is compromised, leading to ischaemia and, if untreated, perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Hydrocele or encysted hydrocele of the cord
Lipoma of the cord or groin
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination in standing and supine positions with cough impulse assessment
Ultrasound of the groin when the diagnosis is uncertain or the swelling is not clinically obvious
CT or MRI in complex, recurrent, or occult hernias
Herniography in selected occult cases (rarely used now)
Baseline bloods and lactate if strangulation or obstruction is suspected
redFlags: Tense, tender, irreducible groin lump with loss of cough impulse indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency)
Features of bowel obstruction (colicky pain, distension, vomiting, absolute constipation) with an irreducible hernia
Overlying skin erythema, systemic sepsis, or rising lactate suggesting strangulated ischaemic bowel
Sudden severe pain in a previously reducible hernia
reference.prognosis: Elective repair has a good outcome with low recurrence after tension-free mesh techniques. Emergency presentation with strangulation carries substantially higher morbidity and mortality, particularly if bowel resection is required in an elderly or comorbid patient.
pitfalls: Mislabelling a femoral hernia as inguinal and underestimating its higher strangulation risk
Attributing a groin lump to a hernia without excluding lymphadenopathy, saphena varix, or vascular causes
Forcible reduction of a strangulated hernia, which can reduce non-viable bowel into the abdomen (reduction en masse)
Failing to identify and address contributing causes of raised intra-abdominal pressure
Delaying surgery in an irreducible, tender hernia and missing evolving strangulation
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Offer elective tension-free mesh repair, by open (Lichtenstein) or laparoscopic approach, as the definitive treatment for symptomatic hernias
Consider watchful waiting for minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic hernias in patients at high operative risk
Undertake emergency surgical exploration for incarcerated or strangulated hernia, with resection of non-viable bowel
Provide perioperative analgesia and advise on avoiding heavy straining during recovery
Refer urgently when a hernia becomes irreducible, tense and tender with loss of cough impulse, signalling obstruction or strangulation
Counsel on the low recurrence rate after mesh repair and give safety-net advice on warning symptoms while awaiting surgery
